title: Selling Skills for Real Estate Professionals
tagline: Earn trust, qualify buyers and tenants, run great viewings, then negotiate fairly, follow up well and protect clients from scams.
description:
Selling or renting property is about people before it is about bricks. Families trust you with one of the biggest decisions of their lives. This quest teaches the everyday skills that turn a new agent into a trusted property professional, with simple steps and local examples from Pakistan.

**Basic stages (free):**

- **The job and trust:** what a property sales professional really does, and how to earn trust from the first call.
- **Finding and qualifying clients:** where leads come from and five friendly questions about need, budget, location, timing and decision-maker.
- **Great viewings:** how to prepare, stay safe and talk about features as benefits.

**Advanced stages (Premium):**

- **Objections and negotiation:** handle concerns calmly and reach a fair close.
- **Follow-up and pipeline:** CRM habits, WhatsApp etiquette, honest listings and photos, and referrals.
- **Ethics and protection:** document checks in general terms, fake files and scams, honest advertising, never promising returns, and building your personal brand.

Rules, fees and procedures differ by city and change over time, so this course teaches skills and always reminds you to check the current rules with the relevant authority or a qualified lawyer. Follow Imran, a new agent in Lahore, as he learns from his mentor Nadia and helps real families find homes safely.
audience: New and aspiring property agents and dealers who want to start well
Sales staff at builders, developers and property portals
Fresh graduates and job seekers considering a career in property sales
Owners who sell or rent out their own property
Anyone who helps family or friends buy, sell or rent property
outcomes: Explain what a property sales professional does and earn trust from the first call
Find and qualify buyers and tenants by need, budget, location, timing and decision-maker
Prepare and run safe, well-planned viewings and present features as benefits
Handle objections with LAER and negotiate to a fair, written close
Keep a simple pipeline, follow up politely on WhatsApp and write honest listings
Protect clients with general document checks, scam awareness and honest advertising
Build a personal brand based on honesty, area knowledge and genuine referrals

Along the way he helps Farhan, a teacher moving from Faisalabad, find a family home, finds a reliable tenant for Rukhsana aunty in Peshawar and learns pipeline habits from Sadia in Karachi. Clear each stage and earn the golden key.

sessions.title: What a Property Sales Professional Does and How to Earn Trust
sessions.summary: Learn what the job really involves, from listening to following through, and why trust is the product you sell. You will practise a first call, be clear about who you work for and learn to say 'I'll check and confirm'.
objectives: Describe the main tasks of a property sales professional
Explain the trust cycle and the habits that keep it turning
Be clear about who you represent and agree fees in writing
Handle a first client call with a clear next step

cards.title: First day at the front desk
cards.setting: Sitara Property Advisors (a fictional agency), Johar Town, Lahore. A Monday morning.

lines.text: Welcome to the Golden Key quest. Your first stop is a small property office in Lahore, where a new agent is about to take his first call.
Nadia baji, the phone has not stopped. Everyone asks for the 'best deal'. I just say yes, yes, we have it!
Saying yes to everything feels good today. Next week it becomes broken promises. Who was that last caller?
A teacher from Faisalabad, Farhan sahib. He is moving to Lahore with his family and wants a house near a school.
Good. Then your job is not to sell him a house today. Your job is to understand his family, tell him the truth and help him decide well.
But how do I earn money if I do not push?
Trust is how you earn money in this work, Imran. One happy family sends you three more. Let me show you what the job really is.

cards.title: What a property sales professional really does

scenes.heading: Listen
scenes.narration: Most of the job is listening. You find out what the client needs, what they can afford, where they want to live and when they must move.

scenes.heading: Match
scenes.narration: You search your listings and your network for options that truly fit. Three good options are better than twenty random ones.

scenes.heading: Show
scenes.narration: You arrange viewings, prepare the property and help the client see how life would feel there, honestly, including the weak points.

scenes.heading: Guide
scenes.narration: You help both sides reach a fair agreement, explain each step in simple words and keep everyone calm.

scenes.heading: Protect
scenes.narration: You push for proper document checks and legal advice before money moves, and you never hide a problem to save a deal.

scenes.heading: Follow through
scenes.narration: After the deal you stay in touch. Happy clients come back and send friends, and that is how a career grows.

cards.title: The trust cycle
cards.caption: Every step feeds the next. Break one, and the cycle slows down.

items.label: Be reachable
items.detail: Answer calls and messages on time, or say clearly when you will reply.

items.label: Tell the truth
items.detail: Share the good and the weak points of every property.

items.label: Keep promises
items.detail: If you say you will call at 5, call at 5.

items.label: Protect the client
items.detail: Put the client's safety and interest before a quick deal.

items.label: Earn referrals
items.detail: Happy clients send family and friends, and the cycle starts again.

cards.question: Farhan asks Imran for 'the best deal in Lahore'. What is the most professional first step?
options: Send him every listing the office has right away
Ask about his family's needs, budget, area and timing
Tell him a deal is available today only
Quote the cheapest house so he stays interested
cards.explanation: You cannot know the best deal for someone until you understand what they need. Listening first saves time for both of you and builds trust from the very first call.

cards.title: Be clear about who you work for
cards.body:
In property sales you might represent different people:

- **The seller or landlord**, who wants a good price and a reliable buyer or tenant.
- **The buyer or tenant**, who wants the right home at a fair price.
- **A builder or developer**, as part of their sales team.
- **A property portal**, helping agents and owners advertise.

Whoever you work for, tell people clearly. If you are paid by the seller, the buyer should know that. How and when you are paid (your commission or fee) should be agreed **in writing** before you start. Practice and rules can differ by city and change over time, so check the current rules with the relevant authority or a qualified lawyer, and never hide your fee inside the price.

cards.back: A property that an owner has asked you to sell or rent, with its details, photos and asking price.
A person who has shown interest, such as a caller, a walk-in or a portal enquiry. Not yet a client.
A planned visit where a buyer or tenant sees the property in person, usually with you.
The owner's permission, ideally written, for you to advertise and show their property.
An early payment to show commitment. Its terms must be written down and checked before any money is paid.
Local area units. Their size can differ between areas and authorities, so always confirm the area in square feet.
The moment the buyer or tenant actually gets the keys and can use the property.

cards.title: Pushy dealer or trusted advisor?
cards.caption: Clients remember how you made them feel long after they forget the price.

items.label: First call
items.left: Talks about his 'hot deal' straight away
items.right: Asks about the family, budget and timing

items.label: Options
items.right: Shares three that truly fit, with reasons

items.label: Weak points
items.left: Hides the damp wall and the noisy road
items.right: Mentions them before the client finds out

items.label: Pressure
items.right: 'Take your time and check the papers'

items.label: After the deal
items.right: Checks in and helps with the move

cards.title: 'Is this the best price in the area?'
cards.situation: Farhan likes a house on Imran's list and asks, 'Imran bhai, is this the best price in this area?' Imran has only worked in this area for one week and does not really know what similar houses have sold for.

choices.text: Say honestly that he will compare similar recent listings and come back with facts by tomorrow.
choices.outcome: Farhan respects the honesty. The next day Imran shares three similar listings and Farhan feels he is getting real advice, not a sales line.

choices.text: Say 'Yes, definitely the best price,' because it sounds confident.
choices.outcome: If Farhan later finds a cheaper similar house, he will doubt everything Imran says. One false claim can cost the whole relationship.

choices.text: Change the subject to the house's nice kitchen.
choices.outcome: Farhan notices the dodge. It avoids a lie, but it does not answer his question or build trust.

cards.title: Builds trust or breaks trust?
cards.prompt: Sort each habit by its effect on clients' trust.

items.text: Calling back at the time you promised
Telling a buyer about a leaking roof before the viewing
Saying 'two other parties are interested' when nobody is
Explaining your fee in writing at the start
Posting old photos that hide new cracks
Saying 'I don't know, I'll check' when you are unsure
Rushing a client to pay before papers are checked

cards.question: Which statement about a new agent's fee is most professional?
options: Mention it only after the deal is done
Add it quietly to the asking price
Assume everyone knows the usual rate
Agree it in writing before starting work
cards.explanation: Fees and commission terms vary, so put them in writing at the start. Hidden or surprise fees damage trust and can cause disputes.

cards.title: Nadia's first-call script
cards.body:
Nadia shares the simple script she has used for years:

1. **Greet and introduce:** 'Assalam-o-alaikum, I am Nadia from Sitara Property Advisors. Thank you for calling.'
2. **Ask, do not pitch:** 'Tell me a little about what you are looking for. Is it for your family or for investment?'
3. **Listen and note:** she writes down the needs, area, budget range and moving date.
4. **Summarise:** 'So you need three bedrooms near a school, in this budget range, by March. Is that right?'
5. **Promise one clear next step:** 'I will send you three suitable options on WhatsApp by 6 pm today.'

Then she does exactly what she promised. That last step is where trust begins.

cards.title: Who wants what most?
cards.prompt: Match each type of client with what usually matters most to them.

pairs.right: Clear explanations and safety at every step
Schools, safety and a reasonable monthly rent
Reliable updates, verified papers and honest photos
A reliable tenant who pays on time and cares for the house
A fair price and a smooth, timely sale

cards.title: Your first client call
cards.prompt: Put the steps of a good first call in order.
steps: Greet the caller and introduce yourself and your office
Ask what they are looking for and why
Listen and note needs, area, budget and timing
Summarise what you heard and check it is right
Agree one clear next step and a time
Do exactly what you promised, on time

cards.title: The 'I will check and confirm' habit
cards.body: You will often be asked things you do not know: the exact size, the age of the building, what similar houses sold for, or what a rule says. Never guess. Say, 'Good question. Let me check and confirm by this evening.' Then write it down and do it. For legal, tax or fee questions, say clearly: 'Please check the current rules with the relevant authority or a qualified lawyer.' Honest uncertainty builds more trust than a confident wrong answer.

cards.title: Remember from The Front Desk
items: The job is to listen, match, show, guide, protect and follow through.
Trust is the real product: be reachable, honest and on time.
Tell people who you work for and agree your fee in writing.
Share weak points of a property before the client finds them.
When unsure, say 'I'll check and confirm' and then do it.
Legal, tax and fee questions go to the relevant authority or a qualified lawyer.

cards.prompt: Think about a time you bought or rented something big, like a phone, a bike or a room. What did the seller do that made you trust or distrust them? Write one habit you will copy and one you will avoid.

quiz.question: What is the main job of a property sales professional on a first call?
options: To close the deal before the call ends
To quote the highest price possible
To listen and understand the client's needs
To send as many listings as possible
quiz.explanation: A first call is for understanding needs, budget, area and timing. Good matching is impossible without good listening.

quiz.question: In the trust cycle, what usually comes after keeping promises and protecting the client?
options: Referrals from happy clients
A higher fee for every deal
Fewer phone calls to answer
Permission to skip document checks
quiz.explanation: When clients feel safe and well served, they send family and friends. Referrals are the reward of trust.

quiz.question: What is a 'lead' in property sales?
options: A signed sale agreement between the buyer and the seller
A property ready for possession
The advance paid by a buyer
A person who has shown interest but is not yet a client
quiz.explanation: A lead is someone who has enquired, such as a caller, a walk-in or a portal enquiry. Qualifying turns some leads into clients.

quiz.question: Why should you confirm a property's area in square feet as well as in marla or kanal?
options: Because marla is no longer used anywhere
Because marla and kanal sizes can differ between areas
Because square feet always make the property sound larger and more valuable
Because portals do not allow local units
quiz.explanation: Local units can mean different sizes in different areas and authorities. Square feet removes confusion and protects both sides.

quiz.question: A buyer asks a question you cannot answer. What is the best response?
options: Say you will check and confirm by a set time
Give your best guess confidently
Say the question does not matter
Ask the buyer to search online instead
quiz.explanation: Honest uncertainty, followed by a quick, accurate answer, builds trust. Guessing can mislead the client.

quiz.question: When should an agent's fee or commission be agreed?
options: Verbally, after the deal closes
Only if the client asks about it
In writing, before the work starts
When the token is being paid
quiz.explanation: Agreeing the fee early and in writing avoids surprises and disputes. Rules and practice vary, so check current requirements.

quiz.question: Which behaviour best shows a trusted advisor rather than a pushy dealer?
options: Saying another buyer is coming today
Mentioning a damp wall before the viewing
Sending twenty listings at once
Avoiding calls after the deal
quiz.explanation: Sharing weak points early shows honesty. Clients trust an agent who tells them what they would otherwise discover later.

quiz.question: Imran sells on behalf of the seller. What should he tell the buyer?
options: Nothing, because it may scare the buyer
That he is fully neutral
That he represents the buyer too
That he represents the seller
quiz.explanation: Being clear about who you work for is basic honesty. The buyer can then judge advice fairly.

quiz.question: A client asks about the exact tax on a property transfer. What should a new agent do?
options: Quote the rate a friend mentioned last year, so the client has a rough idea
Tell them taxes never apply to homes
Promise the seller will pay all of it
Point them to the relevant authority or a qualified lawyer
quiz.explanation: Tax rules and fees change and depend on the case. Agents should not state them as facts; send clients to the right source.

quiz.question: Which first-call ending is strongest?
options: 'Let me know if you need anything'
'I will send three options by 6 pm today'
'Call me whenever you are free'
'I have many houses, just come in'
quiz.explanation: A specific next step with a time shows you listened and that you are reliable. Then you must keep the promise.

sessions.title: Finding and Qualifying Buyers and Tenants
sessions.summary: Find out where good leads come from and how five friendly questions about need, budget, location, timing and decision-maker save everyone time. You will prioritise leads and qualify tenants fairly.
objectives: Name the main sources of property leads
Qualify a lead by need, budget, location, timing and decision-maker
Prioritise leads by urgency and readiness
Qualify tenants fairly while protecting their privacy

cards.title: Forty leads and no viewings
cards.setting: Sitara Property Advisors, Lahore. Late afternoon, a week later.

lines.text: Baji, my portal ad got forty enquiries! I called everyone and showed six houses. Nobody liked anything.
Did you ask them what they needed before the viewings?
Not really. I just sent the address and said 'come and see'.
Then you spent six afternoons guessing. One man wanted a flat near his office. You showed him a house far away.
Assalam-o-alaikum, Nadia beti. I am calling from Peshawar. I need a good tenant for my Lahore house. Last time the tenant left without paying.
Walaikum assalam, Rukhsana aunty. Imran will help, and today he will learn to qualify tenants properly.
Qualify? Like an exam for clients?
Not an exam. Five friendly questions that save everyone time. Let us start.

scenes.heading: Portal enquiries
scenes.narration: People who reply to your online listings. They are many, but they need quick replies and careful qualifying.

scenes.heading: Walk-ins and calls
scenes.narration: People who visit your office or call your signboard. Greet them warmly and take notes.

scenes.heading: Referrals
scenes.narration: Friends and family of happy clients. They often trust you faster because someone vouched for you.

scenes.heading: Social media
scenes.narration: Helpful posts about your area bring messages. Answer politely, never with pressure.

scenes.heading: Past clients
scenes.narration: A tenant today may be a buyer in three years. Keep in touch kindly and they will think of you first.

cards.title: From lead to deal
cards.caption: Not every lead becomes a deal. Qualifying helps you spend time where it matters.

items.label: Leads
items.detail: Everyone who enquired.

items.label: Contacted
items.detail: People you actually spoke to.

items.label: Qualified
items.detail: Clear needs, budget, area, timing and decision-maker.

items.label: Viewings
items.detail: Visits to properties that truly fit.

items.label: Offers
items.detail: Serious discussions on price and terms.

items.label: Deals
items.detail: Signed agreements after proper checks.

cards.question: Why did Imran's six viewings fail?
options: He showed properties before understanding needs
The portal sent him bad leads
He did not use enough photos
Buyers in Lahore never decide quickly
cards.explanation: Without qualifying, viewings are guesses. A few minutes of questions would have matched each person to suitable homes.

cards.title: Five friendly qualifying questions
cards.body:
Before any viewing, try to understand five things. Ask them like a helpful friend, not a form:

- **Need:** 'What kind of place do you need, and why are you moving?'
- **Budget:** 'What range feels comfortable, including other costs?'
- **Location:** 'Which areas suit you, and what must be nearby?'
- **Timing:** 'When do you need to move or decide?'
- **Decision-maker:** 'Who else will help decide? Should they come to the viewing?'

In Pakistan, property decisions are often family decisions. A father, a spouse or a brother abroad may have the final word. Knowing this early saves repeat viewings.

cards.title: Who to call first
cards.caption: Sort qualified leads by how soon they need to move and how ready they are.

items.label: Nurture
items.detail: Ready but not in a hurry. Send updates and good options now and then.

items.label: Call first
items.detail: Ready and needs to move soon. Give them your best time today.

items.label: Low priority
items.detail: Just looking with no clear plan. Stay polite and keep in touch occasionally.

items.label: Help them get ready
items.detail: Needs to move soon but budget or decision is unclear. Ask more questions.

cards.title: The big wish, small budget call
cards.situation: A caller tells Imran he wants a large new house in a top area, with a garden, close to his office, and his budget is much lower than any similar house on the market.

choices.text: Thank him, gently explain what that budget usually gets, and ask which wishes matter most so you can suggest realistic options.
choices.outcome: The caller feels respected. He says a garden matters less than the office distance, and Imran finds two good-fit options in a nearby area.

choices.text: Tell him his budget is a joke and end the call.
choices.outcome: He feels insulted and tells his friends. A rude 'no' loses a future client and a referral.

choices.text: Show him expensive houses anyway, hoping he will stretch his budget.
choices.outcome: He wastes time, feels pressured and may stop trusting Imran. Stretching budgets without care can also hurt the client.

choices.text: Send him all cheap listings in any area without asking more.
choices.outcome: Some might fit, but most will not. Better than rudeness, but it skips the key question of what matters most.

cards.title: Good or poor qualifying question?
cards.prompt: Sort each question by how well it helps you understand the client.

items.text: What must be close to your new home?
You want to buy today, right?
Who else will be part of this decision?
When would you ideally like to move?
Why not just increase your budget?
What did you like or dislike about your current place?
Shall I book you for the most expensive house first?

cards.question: A buyer says, 'My brother in Dubai will decide.' What should Imran do?
options: Ignore it and close with the buyer alone
Stop working with this buyer
Plan to include the brother, for example by video call
Ask the buyer to sign before the brother sees it
cards.explanation: Knowing the decision-maker early saves repeat viewings. Involving the brother respectfully keeps the family together on the decision.

cards.title: Qualifying a tenant for Rukhsana aunty
cards.body:
Imran prepares fair, respectful questions for every tenant who enquires about Rukhsana's house:

- How many people will live in the house?
- Where do you work or study, and how far is it?
- What monthly rent range suits you?
- When would you like to move in?
- Can you share a reference, such as a previous landlord or employer?

He asks every applicant the same questions and treats everyone with equal respect. He keeps their details private and shares them only with Rukhsana. For the tenancy agreement and any registration or police verification steps, he advises her to check the current rules with the relevant authority or a qualified lawyer.

cards.title: Vague answer, better question
cards.prompt: Match each vague answer with a helpful follow-up question.

pairs.right: Which areas do you like, and what must be nearby?
What range would feel comfortable for your family?
Is that within this month, or in the next few months?
How many bedrooms and bathrooms do you need?
What would help you decide? Shall we include your family?

cards.title: A qualifying call, step by step
cards.prompt: Put the steps of a good qualifying call in order.
steps: Thank them for the enquiry and introduce yourself
Ask about their need and reason for moving
Ask about area, budget range and timing
Ask who else will help decide
Summarise and confirm what you heard
Suggest suitable options or a viewing time

cards.title: Talk about the full budget, gently
cards.body: Many buyers think only about the asking price. Remind them gently that buying can also involve other costs, such as taxes, transfer charges, legal fees, repairs or moving. These vary by city, property and time, so do not quote figures as facts. Say, 'Please check the current costs with the relevant authority or a qualified lawyer, so your budget has room for them.' A client who is not surprised later will thank you.

cards.title: Remember from The Lead Market
items: Leads come from portals, walk-ins, referrals, social media and past clients.
Qualify before you show: need, budget, location, timing and decision-maker.
Ask like a helpful friend, not like a form.
Prioritise leads by urgency and readiness.
Treat every applicant fairly and keep their details private.
Remind buyers about other costs, but do not quote figures as facts.

cards.prompt: Think of one person you know who is looking for a house or a room. Write the five qualifying questions you would ask them, in your own friendly words.

quiz.question: What does qualifying a lead mean?
options: Understanding their need, budget, area, timing and decision-maker
Checking if they have a university degree
Asking them to pay a viewing fee
Asking them to pay a viewing fee before you share any listings with them
quiz.explanation: Qualifying means understanding a lead well enough to match them with suitable options and use everyone's time wisely.

quiz.question: Which lead source often trusts you fastest?
options: Random numbers from a phone list
People who saw a street banner once
Referrals from happy past clients
Buyers who called a different office
quiz.explanation: A referral comes with someone's recommendation, so the new client often starts with some trust already.

quiz.question: Which is a good qualifying question?
options: 'You want to sign today, right?'
'Why not increase your budget?'
'Who else will help you decide?'
'Shall I book the priciest house first?'
quiz.explanation: Open, respectful questions reveal real needs. Leading or pushy questions put pressure on the client.

quiz.question: A lead needs to move this month and has a clear budget. Where do they sit in the priority matrix?
options: Call first
Low priority
Nurture only
Ignore until next month
quiz.explanation: High urgency and high readiness means this lead deserves your best time today.

quiz.question: A caller's budget is far below what he wants. What is the best approach?
options: End the call quickly
Show only expensive houses
Promise to find exactly what he wants at that price, whatever it takes
Explain kindly and ask which wishes matter most
quiz.explanation: Respectful honesty plus a priority question helps the client find a realistic option and keeps the relationship.

quiz.question: Why is the decision-maker question important in Pakistan?
options: Only fathers can legally buy property
Property choices are often family decisions
Portals require a decision-maker's name
It lets you skip the buyer
quiz.explanation: Spouses, parents or relatives abroad often have a say. Including them early prevents repeat viewings and surprises.

quiz.question: How should Imran treat different tenant applicants for Rukhsana's house?
options: Ask everyone the same fair questions
Ask harder questions to people he dislikes
Share all applicants' details on WhatsApp groups
Pick the first caller without questions
quiz.explanation: Fair, consistent questions and privacy protect both the landlord and the applicants.

quiz.question: A buyer says 'soon'. What is the best follow-up?
options: 'Great, let us sign tomorrow.'
'Soon is fine, I will wait for you.'
'Is that this month or in a few months?'
'Then you should hurry.'
quiz.explanation: Vague answers need a gentle, specific follow-up. Timing helps you plan and prioritise.

quiz.question: What should an agent say about extra buying costs like taxes and transfer charges?
options: That they are always a fixed amount that every buyer pays the same way
That they vary, so check with the authority or a lawyer
That buyers never pay them
Nothing, to keep the budget simple
quiz.explanation: Remind clients these costs exist, but do not quote figures as facts. Point them to the relevant authority or a qualified lawyer.

quiz.question: Which stage of the funnel comes right before viewings?
options: Deals
Offers
Possession
Qualified
quiz.explanation: In the funnel, leads are contacted, then qualified, and only qualified leads go on to viewings.

sessions.title: Running a Great Viewing and Selling Benefits
sessions.summary: Plan and run viewings that feel like helpful conversations. You will prepare the property and your safety plan, read buyer signals, share weak points honestly and turn features into benefits.
objectives: Prepare a property, the route and a safety plan before a viewing
Turn features into benefits using bridge words
Read buyer signals and respond with good questions
Handle defects honestly and end a viewing with a clear next step

cards.title: Too many facts, not enough feeling
cards.setting: A three-bedroom house for sale, Lahore. Saturday at 11 am.

lines.text: Farhan has brought his wife and two children to see a house that fits their needs and budget. Imran is excited.
Sir, five marla, double storey, three bedrooms, marble floors, a 2019 build, gas, electricity, a water tank, a car porch...
Yes, yes. But will my children be safe walking to school from here?
Er... the school is... somewhere close, I think.
Farhan sahib, the school is a seven-minute walk along a quiet street. Shall we walk it together after we see the rooms?
That is exactly what I wanted to know.
Imran, features are facts about the house. Benefits are what those facts mean for this family. People buy benefits.

cards.title: A great viewing in five scenes

scenes.heading: Prepare
scenes.narration: Check the keys, the route and the timing. Ask the owner to open curtains, switch on lights and tidy up.

scenes.heading: Welcome
scenes.narration: Arrive early. Greet the family, remind them of the main points and ask what they most want to check today.

scenes.heading: Tour
scenes.narration: Let them walk and explore. Point out a few key benefits that match their needs instead of reading a long list.

scenes.heading: Watch and listen
scenes.narration: Notice where they slow down, smile or frown. Ask simple questions like 'How does this room feel for you?'

scenes.heading: Wrap up
scenes.narration: Ask what they liked and what worried them, answer honestly and agree a next step, without pressure.

cards.title: Viewing prep checklist
cards.caption: Ten minutes of preparation saves an hour of awkward surprises.

items.label: Confirm the time
items.detail: With the client and the owner, the day before and again on the day.

items.label: Check access
items.detail: Keys, guard, parking and the exact route.

items.label: Prepare the property
items.detail: Lights on, curtains open, rooms tidy, no strong smells.

items.label: Know the facts
items.detail: Area in square feet, age, utilities, known issues and nearby places.

items.label: Plan for safety
items.detail: Share your location with the office and avoid unknown solo visits.

cards.question: Farhan asks if his children can walk safely to school. What is the best answer?
options: List the marble floors and the car porch
Share the walking time and offer to walk the route
Say 'I think it is close somewhere'
Tell him schools are not your area
cards.explanation: This answers his real need with a fact and a benefit. Offering to walk it together lets him judge for himself.

cards.title: Features, advantages and benefits
cards.body:
A **feature** is a fact about the property. An **advantage** is what that feature does. A **benefit** is what it means for this particular client.

- Feature: a corner house. Advantage: windows on two sides. Benefit: 'Your study room gets morning light for your work.'
- Feature: near the main road. Advantage: easy transport. Benefit: 'Your wife's office is one rickshaw ride away.'

Use the bridge words **'which means'** or **'so that'** to turn a feature into a benefit. Choose the benefits that match what the client told you while qualifying. Never invent a benefit you cannot back up.

cards.title: Turn the feature into a benefit

cards.back: Easy for your elderly parents: no stairs to climb every day.
Room for the whole family at Eid without feeling crowded.
Your car stays cooler in summer and safer from rain.
Daily shopping on foot, so less time stuck in traffic.
You can rent out the upper portion while keeping your privacy.
Cooler rooms and fresher air on hot days.

cards.title: Telling or asking?
cards.caption: Good viewings feel like a conversation, not a lecture.

items.label: Kitchen
items.right: 'Who cooks most at home? Is this space enough?'

items.label: Area
items.right: 'Shall we see the walk to the school?'

items.label: Weak point
items.right: 'This wall needs repair; let us check how serious it is.'

cards.title: The damp patch
cards.situation: During the viewing, Farhan's wife notices a damp patch near the bathroom ceiling. The owner told Imran that morning there was 'a small old leak, now fixed', but Imran has not seen proof.

choices.text: Share what the owner said, say he has not seen proof, and suggest a proper check by a plumber before any decision.
choices.outcome: The family feels respected. They ask the owner for repair receipts and an inspection. Whatever they decide, they trust Imran.

choices.text: Say 'Oh, that is nothing, it is fixed,' as if he is sure.
choices.outcome: If the leak returns after they move in, the family will feel cheated and will warn others about Imran.

choices.text: Say he will ask the owner and let them know later.
choices.outcome: Better than hiding it, but it misses the chance to share what he already knows and suggest a proper check.

cards.title: Before, during or after the viewing?
cards.prompt: Sort each task into the right moment.

items.text: Confirm the time with the owner
Share your location with the office
Watch where the family slows down
Ask 'How does this room feel for you?'
Send a thank-you message and a summary
Answer the questions you promised to check
Point out benefits that match their needs
Ask the owner to open curtains and switch on lights

cards.question: Which sentence turns a feature into a benefit?
options: 'It is near the market.'
'The market is very famous.'
'Many shops are in this area, sir.'
'It is near the market, so you can shop on foot'
cards.explanation: The bridge 'so you can' connects the fact to what it means in the client's daily life.

cards.title: Benefit talk for a young couple
cards.body:
Sadia, a sales executive at a fictional developer in Karachi, shows a two-bedroom flat to a young couple. While qualifying, she learned they both work, they want to save money and they plan to start a family.

Instead of reading the brochure, she says:

- 'The bus stop is right outside, which means you can share one car and save on fuel.'
- 'The second bedroom is next to yours, so it can become a nursery later.'
- 'There is a lift and a ramp, so moving a pram will be easy.'

When the husband asks about the building's approvals, she says, 'Here are the documents we have. Please have a qualified lawyer check them and confirm with the relevant authority.'

cards.title: Read the buyer's signals
cards.prompt: Match each signal with what it may mean and how to respond.

pairs.left: Measuring a room with a phone
pairs.right: Imagining their furniture: ask what they plan to put there
Something worries them: gently ask what they think
Strong interest: ask what they like about it
Thinking about daily life: share honest, general facts
Short on time: focus on their top needs and wrap up

cards.title: The flow of a good viewing
cards.prompt: Put the stages of a viewing in order.
steps: Confirm time, access and safety plan
Arrive early and prepare the property
Welcome the client and ask what matters most today
Let them explore while you point out matching benefits
Ask what they liked and what worried them
Agree a next step and send a summary message

cards.title: Stay safe at viewings
cards.body: Property work means meeting strangers in empty buildings. Keep simple habits: meet new clients at the office first when you can, share your location and viewing time with a colleague, prefer daylight, keep your phone charged and trust your instincts. If something feels wrong, end the visit politely. These habits protect you, the owner and the client.

cards.title: Remember from The Open House
items: Prepare the property, the route, the facts and your safety plan.
Let clients explore; point out a few benefits that match their needs.
Features are facts; benefits are what those facts mean for this client.
Use bridge words like 'which means' and 'so that'.
Ask questions and read signals instead of reading a long list.
Share weak points honestly and suggest proper checks.

cards.prompt: Pick a room in your own home. Write three features of it, then turn each one into a benefit for a family you can imagine, using 'which means' or 'so that'.

quiz.question: What is a 'benefit' in property sales?
options: The asking price after discount
A list of the property's facts
The fee the agent receives
What a feature means for this client's life
quiz.explanation: Features are facts. Benefits connect those facts to the client's own needs and daily life.

quiz.question: Which is a feature, not a benefit?
options: 'Your car stays cool in summer.'
'The house has a covered car porch.'
'Your parents avoid stairs every day.'
'Your children can walk to school.'
quiz.explanation: A covered car porch is a fact about the house. The others explain what such facts mean for the client.

quiz.question: Which bridge words help turn a feature into a benefit?
options: 'which means' or 'so that'
'however' or 'although'
'trust me' or 'believe me'
'by the way' or 'anyway'
quiz.explanation: These bridge words naturally connect a fact to its effect on the client.

quiz.question: What should you do before a viewing?
options: Arrive late so the owner can tidy
Avoid telling anyone where you are
Confirm the time and access with owner and client
Prepare a long list of every feature so you can read it out room by room
quiz.explanation: Confirming time, keys and route avoids wasted trips and shows professionalism.

quiz.question: A buyer goes quiet in one room. What is the best response?
options: Move quickly to the next room
Talk more about the marble floors
Gently ask what they think of it
Tell them it is the best room
quiz.explanation: Silence can signal a worry. A gentle question invites them to share it so you can respond honestly.

quiz.question: A buyer spots a damp patch you were told is 'fixed', without proof. What should you do?
options: Share what you know and suggest a proper check
Say confidently it is nothing
Change the topic to the garden so the family focuses on the good points
Advise them to decide quickly
quiz.explanation: Share facts honestly, admit what you have not verified and suggest an inspection before any decision.

quiz.question: Which is a good viewing safety habit?
options: Meet unknown clients alone at night
Leave your phone in the car
Keep your plans secret from the office
Share your location and time with a colleague
quiz.explanation: Simple safety habits protect agents, owners and clients when meeting new people in empty properties.

quiz.question: Why does Nadia offer to walk the route to the school with Farhan?
options: It fills time before the price talk
It lets him judge his top need himself
It avoids showing the bedrooms
It is required by every agency rule
quiz.explanation: Seeing the route for himself answers his real worry far better than words.

quiz.question: What is the best way to end a viewing?
options: Ask what they liked and worried about, then agree a next step
Ask them to pay a token on the spot so the house is held for them
Leave without any follow-up plan
Tell them another family is coming
quiz.explanation: A calm wrap-up surfaces concerns, keeps trust and moves things forward without pressure.

quiz.question: Asked about a building's approvals, which reply is best?
options: 'All approvals are complete, trust me'
'Approvals do not matter for flats, only for houses and plots in societies'
'Here are our documents; please have a lawyer check them'
'Our brochure says it is approved'
quiz.explanation: Share what you have and encourage independent checks with a qualified lawyer and the relevant authority.

sessions.title: Handling Objections and Negotiating to a Fair Close
sessions.summary: Step up to Advanced. Use LAER to handle objections, spot smoke screens, prepare for negotiation, make fair trades and close in writing, with legal checks before any money moves.
objectives: Handle objections with listen, acknowledge, explore and respond
Tell real objections from smoke screens
Prepare and negotiate using fair trades, not tricks
Close a deal in writing with proper checks and traceable payments

cards.title: The price is too high
cards.setting: Sitara Property Advisors, Lahore. Tuesday evening, three days after the viewing.

lines.text: Imran bhai, we love the house. But the price is too high for us. We cannot go that far.
Sir, I understand... (whispering to Nadia) Baji, should I tell him another party is ready to pay more? Then he will hurry.
Is there another party?
No... not really.
Then never say it. A fake buyer is a lie, and lies come back. An objection is not a 'no'. It is a question we have not answered yet.
So what can we do?
Let us understand the gap first, Farhan sahib. Then we will see what is fair for both your family and the seller.

cards.title: LAER: four steps for any objection

scenes.heading: Listen
scenes.narration: Let the client finish. Do not jump in with an answer while they are still speaking.

scenes.heading: Acknowledge
scenes.narration: Show you understand: 'I hear you, the price feels high for your budget.' This is not agreeing, it is respecting.

scenes.heading: Explore
scenes.narration: Ask questions to find the real concern: 'Is it the total price, the monthly cost, or how it compares with other houses?'

scenes.heading: Respond
scenes.narration: Answer the real concern with facts, options or a fair trade. Then check: 'Does that help?'

cards.title: The objection loop
cards.caption: Go round the loop until the real concern is answered or you both agree it cannot be.

items.label: Listen
items.detail: Let them speak fully.

items.label: Acknowledge
items.detail: Show you understand the feeling.

items.label: Explore
items.detail: Find the real concern with questions.

items.label: Respond
items.detail: Answer with facts, options or a fair trade.

items.label: Check
items.detail: Ask if that answers the concern.

cards.question: A buyer says the price is too high. What should Imran do first?
options: Listen fully and acknowledge the concern
Say another buyer will pay more
Lower the price without asking the seller
Tell the buyer the price is fair, end of story
cards.explanation: LAER starts with listening and acknowledging. Only then can you explore the real concern and respond well.

cards.title: Real objections and smoke screens
cards.body:
Common objections in property sales include **price**, **location**, **condition**, **timing**, **trust** and **'I need to ask my family'**.

Some are **real**: the budget truly does not stretch. Some are **smoke screens**: a polite way of hiding a different worry, such as doubts about the papers or the neighbourhood.

To tell the difference, ask an open question: 'If the price were right, is there anything else stopping you?' If the answer is 'No', the price is the real issue. If they pause, there is another worry. Answer that one first.

cards.title: Objection and a good response
cards.prompt: Match each objection with a helpful, honest response.

pairs.right: 'Let us compare it with similar recent listings together'

pairs.left: 'It is too far from my office'
pairs.right: 'Shall we check the travel time at rush hour?'
'Of course. Would a video tour or a second visit help them?'

pairs.left: 'I am not sure the papers are clean'
pairs.right: 'Please have a qualified lawyer check them before any payment'
'No problem. What would need to happen first?'

cards.title: Prepare before you negotiate
cards.caption: Most negotiations are won or lost before anyone sits down.

items.label: Know the facts
items.detail: Similar listings, the property's condition and its documents.

items.label: Know each side's needs
items.detail: Price matters, but so do timing, possession and fixtures.

items.label: Know the limits
items.detail: Each side's walk-away point, which you never reveal without permission.

items.label: Plan fair trades
items.detail: What each side could give that costs them little but helps the other.

items.label: Agree in writing
items.detail: Write down agreed terms clearly before anyone pays.

cards.title: What kind of deal is this?
cards.caption: Aim for the top right: both sides feel the outcome is fair.

items.label: Buyer wins, seller loses
items.detail: Seller feels cheated and may back out later.

items.label: Both win
items.detail: A fair deal both sides will honour and recommend.

items.label: Both lose
items.detail: Nobody is happy; the deal often falls apart.

items.label: Seller wins, buyer loses
items.detail: Buyer feels pushed and will not come back.

cards.title: The fake second buyer
cards.situation: The seller tells Imran, 'Tell Farhan another party has offered more. That will make him pay my price.' There is no other party. Imran's monthly target is close, and the seller is a regular client of the office.

choices.text: Politely refuse to invent a buyer, explain it would damage trust, and suggest working on fair trades instead.
choices.outcome: The seller grumbles but agrees. Imran helps both sides find a fair middle with earlier possession for the seller. Both later recommend him.

choices.text: Say it, because the seller asked and it is not Imran's lie.
choices.outcome: It is still Imran's lie. If Farhan finds out, he walks away and tells others. The office's name suffers too.

choices.text: Avoid saying it directly but hint that 'interest is high' this week.
choices.outcome: A vague hint is still misleading. It may work once but it chips away at your honesty.

choices.text: Tell Nadia and ask how the office handles such requests.
choices.outcome: A reasonable step that brings in experience, but Imran should also be ready to refuse clearly himself.

cards.title: Fair tactic or unfair tactic?
cards.prompt: Sort each negotiation move.

items.text: Comparing similar recent listings openly
Inventing a competing buyer
Offering earlier possession in return for price flexibility
Hiding a known defect to keep the price high
Taking a pause to let both sides think
Pressuring a buyer to pay before checking papers
Writing down agreed terms for both sides to read

cards.question: In a negotiation, what is a 'fair trade'?
options: One side gives everything and the other gives nothing
The agent decides the final price alone
Each side gives something that costs them little but helps the other
The buyer pays more to finish faster, always
cards.explanation: Good trades, such as flexible possession dates or included fixtures, create value for both sides and help reach a fair close.

cards.title: Closing the gap for Farhan
cards.body:
Farhan's offer and the seller's price are still apart. Imran explores both sides:

- **Seller:** needs to move to Islamabad within six weeks and does not want to take the air conditioners and kitchen fittings.
- **Farhan:** has a fixed budget, but can move any time and can pay quickly once papers are checked.

Imran suggests a trade: the seller reduces the price a little; the fittings stay; Farhan agrees to a quick, fixed timeline. Both agree. Imran writes the terms in a clear summary for both sides and says, 'Before any token or payment, please have a qualified lawyer check the documents and the agreement.'

cards.title: Steps to a fair close
cards.prompt: Put the closing steps in order.
steps: Summarise the terms both sides have agreed
Confirm each side understands and accepts them
Write the terms down clearly
Have documents and the agreement checked by a qualified lawyer
Make payments only through traceable channels, with receipts
Agree dates for the next steps and possession

cards.title: Trade, do not just give
cards.body: When someone asks for a discount, do not simply say yes or no. Ask, 'If the seller can move on price, could you be flexible on the possession date?' Trading keeps the deal balanced and shows both sides that every change has a reason. Also, do not fear silence: after you make a fair proposal, stop talking and let people think.

cards.question: Which is the strongest sign that a negotiation ended well?
options: The buyer paid the highest possible price
Both sides feel it was fair and would recommend you
The agent finished it in one day
The seller did not need to sign anything
cards.explanation: A deal both sides see as fair is more likely to be honoured and to bring you future referrals.

cards.title: Remember from The Negotiation Table
items: An objection is a question you have not answered yet.
Use LAER: listen, acknowledge, explore, respond, then check.
Find out whether an objection is real or a smoke screen.
Prepare: facts, needs, limits, fair trades and written terms.
Never invent buyers, hide defects or rush payments.
Close only after papers are checked by a qualified lawyer and payments are traceable.

cards.prompt: Recall a time someone tried to pressure you into buying something. How did it feel? Write how you would handle the same moment if you were the seller, using LAER.

quiz.question: What does the 'A' in LAER stand for?
options: Agree
Acknowledge
Argue
Accept the price
quiz.explanation: Acknowledge means showing you understand the concern. It is respect, not necessarily agreement.

quiz.question: Why is inventing a competing buyer wrong?
options: It is only wrong if the buyer is rich
It never works on buyers
It slows the deal too much
It is a lie that damages trust
quiz.explanation: A fake buyer is deception. When found out, it destroys trust in the agent and the office.

quiz.question: Which question helps uncover a smoke screen objection?
options: 'Why are you being difficult?'
'Can you sign by tonight?'
'Can you sign by tonight, because I may not be able to hold this price for long?'
'If the price were right, would anything else stop you?'
quiz.explanation: This open question tests whether price is the real concern or a cover for another worry.

quiz.question: In the deal matrix, which outcome should a professional aim for?
options: The seller gets everything
Both sides feel the deal is fair
The buyer pays the least possible
The agent earns the most possible
quiz.explanation: A fair outcome for both sides is more likely to be honoured and to bring referrals.

quiz.question: Which is an example of a fair trade in negotiation?
options: Earlier possession in return for price flexibility
Hiding defects for a higher price
Paying a token before papers are checked
Promising the buyer future profits
quiz.explanation: Trades exchange things each side values differently, so both gain something.

quiz.question: When should a buyer pay a token or advance?
options: Immediately at the first viewing, so the seller knows the buyer is serious
Whenever the agent asks for it
After documents and the agreement are checked by a lawyer
Before the seller shows any documents
quiz.explanation: Money should move only after proper checks, with clear written terms and traceable payment.

quiz.question: A buyer says, 'I need to ask my family.' What is a helpful reply?
options: 'Your family will only slow this down.'
'Decide alone, it is your money, and families always slow these things down.'
'Would a video tour or a second visit help them?'
'This offer ends in one hour.'
quiz.explanation: Respecting family decisions and making it easy for them to see the property keeps trust and momentum.

quiz.question: What should you do right after making a fair proposal?
options: Pause and let both sides think
Keep talking to fill the silence
Raise the price immediately
Leave the meeting quickly
quiz.explanation: Silence gives people time to consider. Rushing in often weakens a good proposal.

quiz.question: Which part of negotiation preparation should you never reveal without permission?
options: The property's known defects
The written terms
Similar recent listings
A side's walk-away limit
quiz.explanation: Each side's limits are confidential. Defects, terms and market comparisons should be shared openly.

quiz.question: How should payments in a property deal be made?
options: In cash, with no record
Through traceable channels, with receipts
To the agent's personal account
Through any friend who offers
quiz.explanation: Traceable payments with receipts protect everyone and make disputes easier to resolve.

sessions.title: Follow-Up, Pipeline and Referrals
sessions.summary: Stop losing good leads. Build a simple pipeline with CRM habits, follow up with value, use WhatsApp professionally, write honest portal listings with good photos and grow through referrals.
objectives: Keep a simple pipeline with stages, next steps and dates
Follow up politely and usefully after viewings
Use WhatsApp professionally and protect client privacy
Write honest listings with clear, real photos and ask for referrals well

cards.title: The buyer who went to someone else
cards.setting: Sitara Property Advisors, Lahore, and a video call with Karachi.

lines.text: Baji, the family I showed the flat to last month bought through another agent. They said I never called back!
Did you call back?
I meant to... but I had so many leads. I forgot who was who.
Imran, I had the same problem when I joined our developer's sales team in Karachi. Then I started a simple pipeline.
A pipeline? Like water?
Like a path every client walks along. I write each one down, with the next step and a date. Nobody gets forgotten now.
Good leads are hard to find and easy to lose. Today you learn to keep them.

scenes.heading: Capture
scenes.narration: Every new lead goes into one place the same day: a CRM, a spreadsheet or even a notebook. Name, number, source and needs.

scenes.heading: Tag the stage
scenes.narration: Mark where they are: new, contacted, qualified, viewing done, negotiating, closed or lost.

scenes.heading: Set the next step
scenes.narration: Every lead gets one next action and a date, such as 'send two options by Thursday'.

scenes.heading: Follow up
scenes.narration: Do the next step on time. Short, helpful, polite messages beat long sales speeches.

scenes.heading: Review weekly
scenes.narration: Each week, look at the whole list. Who is stuck? Who needs a call? Who should be closed politely?

cards.title: Stages in a simple pipeline
cards.caption: Move each client to the next stage only when the step is truly done.

items.label: New
items.detail: Captured with name, number, source and needs.

items.label: Contacted
items.detail: You have spoken and introduced yourself.

items.label: Qualified
items.detail: Need, budget, area, timing and decision-maker are clear.

items.label: Viewing done
items.detail: They have seen at least one suitable property.

items.label: Negotiating
items.detail: Price and terms are being discussed.

items.label: Closed
items.detail: Deal done after proper checks, or politely marked lost with a reason.

cards.question: What is the most important field to fill for every lead in a pipeline?
options: Their favourite colour
How rich they look
The number of times they said no
The next step and its date
cards.explanation: A lead without a next step and date is easy to forget. This one field keeps your follow-up on track.

cards.title: Simple CRM habits that work
cards.body:
A CRM (customer relationship management tool) is simply an organised list of your clients and what happens with them. It can be an app, a spreadsheet or a notebook. The habits matter more than the tool:

- **One place:** do not scatter leads across chats, papers and memory.
- **Same-day entry:** add every lead the day you meet them.
- **Notes after every call:** two lines on what was said and agreed.
- **Next step and date:** always.
- **Privacy:** client numbers and details are private. Do not share them in groups, sell them or use them for anything the client did not agree to.

Features of CRM apps differ by product and plan, so check the current terms of any tool you choose.

cards.title: Follow-up after a viewing
cards.caption: A gentle rhythm keeps you remembered without being annoying.

items.label: Same day
items.detail: Thank them and send a short summary of what they saw.

items.label: Within two days
items.detail: Answer any questions you promised to check.

items.label: About a week
items.detail: Check in: 'Have you had time to discuss it with the family?'

items.label: When something new fits
items.detail: Share a new option that matches their needs.

items.label: After the deal
items.detail: Help with the move and check that all is well.

items.label: Months later
items.detail: A friendly hello and, when the time is right, ask for a referral.

cards.back: Message during reasonable hours. Avoid late nights, early mornings and prayer or meal times when you can.
Start with your name and office, even if you spoke yesterday. Clients talk to many agents.
Use short text for key facts like addresses and times. Send voice notes only if the client is happy with them.
Send listings only to people who asked, and stop if they ask you to.
Never add clients to groups or forward their numbers without permission.
Share clear, honest photos and a location pin so clients do not get lost.

cards.title: The client who went quiet
cards.situation: After a good viewing, a couple stops replying to Imran's messages. It has been ten days. Imran has sent four messages already, each saying 'Sir, any update?'

choices.text: Send one short, helpful message with something useful, such as a new similar option, and say he will not disturb them further unless they reply.
choices.outcome: The couple replies two days later. They were busy with a family wedding. They appreciate that Imran was polite and gave them value.

choices.text: Keep messaging every day until they answer.
choices.outcome: The couple feels chased and blocks his number. Persistence without value becomes spam.

choices.text: Stop all contact forever without a word.
choices.outcome: Not harmful, but he may lose a buyer who was simply busy. One polite, useful message would have been better.

cards.title: WhatsApp do or don't?
cards.prompt: Sort each message habit.

items.text: Start with your name and office
Send a location pin before a viewing
Add clients to a big listings group without asking
Send ten voice notes in a row at midnight
Confirm the viewing time in writing
Forward one client's number to another dealer
Stop sending listings when asked

cards.question: Which follow-up message is best a week after a viewing?
options: 'Have you had time to discuss it with the family?'
'Sir, any update? Any update?'
'Last chance, it will be sold tomorrow!'
'Why are you not answering me?'
cards.explanation: A warm, specific check-in respects the client's process. Fake urgency or pushy messages damage trust.

cards.title: An honest portal listing
cards.body:
Imran writes a listing for Rukhsana's house on a property portal. Portal features and rules differ, so he checks the current terms on the platform first.

- **Title:** '3-bed house for rent near a park, quiet street'.
- **Facts:** area in square feet as well as the local unit, number of rooms, floor, utilities and parking.
- **Benefits:** 'Park two minutes away, so children can play safely.'
- **Honest notes:** 'Kitchen is older but clean and working.'
- **Photos:** recent, bright and real. No filters that change colours, and no photos of a different house.
- **Contact:** his name, office and the times he answers.

When the house is rented, he marks the listing as taken the same day.

cards.title: Photo problem and fix
cards.prompt: Match each listing photo problem with a fix.

pairs.right: Shoot in daylight with curtains open and lights on
Hold the phone straight at chest height
Ask the owner to tidy before the shoot
Show whole rooms so buyers understand the space
Never use them; take real, recent photos only

cards.title: Taking listing photos
cards.prompt: Put the photo steps in order.
steps: Get the owner's permission and agree a time
Ask for the property to be tidied and lights switched on
Shoot each room from a corner, phone held straight
Take photos of the outside, the street and key features
Choose clear, honest photos and skip misleading ones
Upload them with accurate facts and mark the listing taken when done

cards.title: Ask for referrals at the right moment
cards.body: The best moment to ask for a referral is when a client is happy: at key handover, after a smooth move or when they thank you. Keep it simple: 'I am glad this went well. If anyone in your family or office is looking, I would be happy to help them too.' Thank people who refer you, and keep them updated. If you plan to give any thank-you reward, tell the new client openly. Never pressure anyone.

cards.title: Remember from The Pipeline Room
items: Put every lead in one place the same day.
Every lead needs a stage, a next step and a date.
Follow up with value, not with 'any update?' spam.
Follow WhatsApp etiquette: timing, introductions, privacy and consent.
Write honest listings with real, recent, clear photos.
Ask for referrals when clients are happy, and thank people openly.

cards.prompt: List five people you have spoken to about property, a job or a business in the last month. For each, write the next step and a date. How many would you have forgotten without writing them down?

quiz.question: What is a CRM in simple terms?
options: An organised list of clients and what happens with them
A government property registration form that every agent must fill in
A type of portal advertisement
A legal agreement between agents
quiz.explanation: A CRM can be an app, a spreadsheet or a notebook. It keeps client details, stages and next steps organised.

quiz.question: When should a new lead be added to your pipeline?
options: Only after they sign a deal
At the end of the month
The same day you meet them
When they call you a second time
quiz.explanation: Same-day entry stops leads from being lost in chats and memory.

quiz.question: Which WhatsApp habit is most professional?
options: Sending voice notes late at night
Starting with your name and office
Adding clients to groups without asking
Forwarding numbers to other dealers
quiz.explanation: Clients talk to many agents. Introducing yourself every time makes your message clear and respectful.

quiz.question: A client stops replying after a viewing. What is the best action?
options: Message them daily until they answer
Call their office to find them
Tell them the house is almost sold
Send one helpful message, then wait
quiz.explanation: One polite message with something useful respects their time and keeps the door open.

quiz.question: Which listing photo practice is honest?
options: Photos of a nicer house nearby
Heavy filters that change colours
Old photos from before repairs were needed
Real, recent photos taken in daylight
quiz.explanation: Honest photos build trust and prevent wasted viewings and complaints.

quiz.question: Why should you mark a listing as taken as soon as it is sold or rented?
options: So the portal charges you less for the listings you still keep online
So people are not misled by an unavailable property
So competitors cannot see it
Because photos expire automatically
quiz.explanation: Leaving taken properties online misleads people and harms your reputation. Portal rules also vary, so check them.

quiz.question: What is the best moment to ask for a referral?
options: When the client is happy, such as at handover
At the very first call
Just after an argument over price
Before the client has seen any property
quiz.explanation: People refer you when they have had a good experience. Ask simply and never pressure.

quiz.question: What should you do with clients' phone numbers?
options: Share them in dealer groups so other agents can help find matching properties
Sell them to other agencies
Keep them private and use them only as agreed
Post them with listings
quiz.explanation: Client details are private. Using them only for what the client agreed to protects trust.

quiz.question: In a weekly pipeline review, what should you look for first?
options: Leads with the longest names
Leads from the richest areas only
Leads stuck without a next step
Leads you liked chatting with
quiz.explanation: A weekly review finds stuck or forgotten leads so you can act or close them politely.

quiz.question: If you plan to give someone a thank-you reward for a referral, what should you do?
options: Tell the new client openly
Keep it secret from everyone
Add it to the client's price quietly
Pay it only in cash with no record
quiz.explanation: Openness about any referral reward keeps your advice trusted and avoids hidden conflicts of interest.

sessions.title: Ethics, Document Checks, Protecting Clients and Your Personal Brand
sessions.summary: Protect clients and your name. Learn general document and approval checks, the warning signs of fake files and scams, honest advertising, why you never promise returns, and how to build a personal brand on trust.
objectives: Explain general checks on the seller, property, approvals and payment path
Recognise warning signs of fake files and property scams
Advertise honestly and never promise investment returns
Build a personal brand based on honesty and area knowledge

cards.title: The file that was too good to be true
cards.setting: Farhan's new home, Lahore. Two months after the move.

lines.text: Imran bhai, my cousin saw an ad for a plot file in a new society. Very cheap, and it says profit will double in one year! Should he buy?
Doubling in one year? Who is promising that?
A dealer on social media. He wants the payment by tonight to his personal account. No office visit needed.
Farhan sahib, please ask your cousin to stop and not pay anything yet. Those are warning signs.
Cheap price, guaranteed profit, rush, a personal account and no office. That is five red flags.
Well spotted, Imran. Protecting clients from scams is part of our job, even when we earn nothing from it.
That is why I trust you two.

cards.title: Five checks before any money moves

scenes.heading: Check the seller
scenes.narration: Make sure the person selling is the real owner, or has proper written authority, and that their identity matches the ownership papers.

scenes.heading: Check the property
scenes.narration: Ask for the original ownership documents and have their record confirmed with the relevant land record office or authority.

scenes.heading: Check the approvals
scenes.narration: For a project or society, check its approval status directly with the relevant development authority, not just the brochure.

scenes.heading: Check the payment path
scenes.narration: Pay only through traceable channels to the right party, with receipts. Be careful with requests to pay personal accounts.

scenes.heading: Get legal advice
scenes.narration: Ask a qualified lawyer to check the documents and the agreement. Rules change, so always check the current rules.

cards.title: A document check, in general terms
cards.caption: Exact documents and procedures vary by city and authority. Confirm the current steps with the relevant authority or a qualified lawyer.

items.label: Collect copies
items.detail: Ownership papers, the seller's identity documents and any previous transfer papers.

items.label: Match the names
items.detail: The seller's identity should match the ownership record.

items.label: Verify the record
items.detail: Confirm ownership and any dues or disputes with the relevant office.

items.label: Verify approvals
items.detail: For new projects, confirm approval status directly with the relevant authority.

items.label: Legal review
items.detail: A qualified lawyer checks everything and the draft agreement.

items.label: Pay safely
items.detail: Traceable payments, receipts and a written agreement.

cards.question: A seller shows only photocopies and refuses to show originals. What should Imran advise?
options: Pay a small token to keep the deal
Trust the seller because he seems polite
Pause, and ask a qualified lawyer to guide the checks
Ignore it, photocopies are always enough
cards.explanation: Refusing to show original documents is a warning sign. Pause and get proper legal guidance before any payment.

cards.title: Fake files and common scams
cards.body:
In Pakistan, some housing projects sell **files**: a document that promises a plot or unit in future. Some files are genuine; others are linked to projects that do not have the land or approvals they claim, or the same file is sold to more than one person.

Warning signs of a scam:

- A price far below similar properties.
- **Guaranteed** profit or 'double in a year'.
- Pressure to pay today.
- Payment to a personal account or in cash with no receipt.
- No proper office, or reluctance to show documents.
- Approval claims you cannot confirm with the relevant authority.

When in doubt, stop, verify and ask a qualified lawyer.

cards.title: Red flag or normal?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation.

items.text: Guaranteed double profit in one year
Seller shares original documents for checking
Payment requested to a personal account tonight
Buyer's lawyer reviews the agreement
Price far below every similar property
Approval claimed but not confirmable with the authority
Written agreement with clear terms and dates
Receipt given for every payment

cards.title: Honest ad or misleading ad?
cards.caption: Your ads are promises. Make only the ones you can keep.

items.label: Price
items.left: Real asking price, or clearly 'price on request'
items.right: A bait price for a house that does not exist

items.label: Photos
items.right: Photos of a different or edited property

items.label: Returns
items.left: 'Ask a qualified adviser about investment risk'

items.label: Approvals
items.left: 'Please verify approvals with the relevant authority'
items.right: 'Fully approved' with no way to check

items.label: Availability
items.left: Marked taken as soon as it is sold

cards.title: The returns promise
cards.situation: A sales manager at a fictional developer asks Imran to post ads saying, 'Invest now, guaranteed high returns within two years!' Imran is promised a bonus for every booking.

choices.text: Refuse to promise returns, explain that property values can go down as well as up, and offer to write ads about real features and benefits instead.
choices.outcome: The manager is unhappy at first, but Imran keeps his name clean. Buyers who come to him trust that his ads are honest.

choices.text: Post the ads, because the manager takes responsibility.
choices.outcome: Imran's name is on the ads. If buyers lose money, they will blame him, and promising returns can mislead people badly.

choices.text: Post the ads but add very small text saying 'terms apply'.
choices.outcome: Tiny disclaimers do not fix a misleading headline. It is still a promise he cannot keep.

choices.text: Ask the manager for written proof behind the claim before deciding.
choices.outcome: A sensible question, but even with forecasts, nobody can guarantee future property returns. The best answer is not to promise them.

cards.title: Situation and the ethical action
cards.prompt: Match each situation with the right professional action.

pairs.left: You represent the seller and the buyer
pairs.right: Tell both sides clearly and get their agreement
Disclose it before the buyer decides

pairs.left: A client asks about tax or fees
pairs.right: Point them to the relevant authority or a qualified lawyer

pairs.left: A deal looks like a scam
pairs.right: Stop, warn the client and advise proper checks
Explain that nobody can guarantee property returns

pairs.left: A colleague shares client data in a group
pairs.right: Raise it, because client details must stay private

cards.question: Which claim should an honest property professional never make?
options: 'Please verify the approvals yourself'
'This investment is guaranteed to double'
'The kitchen is older but works well'
'The area is in square feet and marla'
cards.explanation: Nobody can guarantee property returns. Promising them misleads clients and can cause serious losses.

cards.title: Imran's personal brand plan
cards.body:
After six months, Imran writes a simple plan to become known as a trusted agent in his area:

- **Focus:** one or two areas he knows deeply: streets, schools, markets and common issues.
- **Consistent profile:** the same name, photo, office and contact hours on WhatsApp, portals and social media.
- **Helpful content:** short posts like 'Five questions to ask before renting' and 'Why to check documents with a lawyer'. No hype, no guaranteed returns.
- **Honest reviews:** he asks happy clients to share genuine feedback and never writes fake reviews.
- **Learning:** he keeps learning about rules and processes, and still tells clients to check the current rules with the relevant authority or a qualified lawyer.

cards.title: Building a personal brand
cards.caption: Build from the bottom up. Without honesty at the base, the rest falls down.

items.label: Referrals and reputation
items.detail: People recommend you by name.

items.label: Helpful content
items.detail: Simple, honest posts that teach clients something useful.

items.label: Consistent presence
items.detail: Same name, photo, contact details and tone everywhere.

items.label: Area knowledge
items.detail: Deep, practical knowledge of the areas you work in.

items.label: Honesty
items.detail: Truthful ads, fair advice and protecting clients, always.

cards.title: Before a client pays a token
cards.prompt: Put these protective steps in order.
steps: Confirm the seller's identity matches the ownership record
Verify the property record and approvals with the relevant authority
Have a qualified lawyer review documents and the draft agreement
Write down agreed price, dates and conditions clearly
Pay through a traceable channel to the right party
Keep receipts and copies of every document

cards.title: Say the safe sentence
cards.body: Learn one sentence by heart and use it often: 'Rules, fees and procedures can change, so please check the current rules with the relevant authority or a qualified lawyer.' It protects your client, protects you and shows you take their safety seriously. A good agent knows the process in general; a good lawyer confirms the details for each case.

cards.title: Remember from The Trust Vault
items: Check the seller, the property, the approvals and the payment path before money moves.
Ask a qualified lawyer to review documents and agreements.
Learn the warning signs of fake files and scams.
Advertise honestly: real prices, real photos, no bait listings.
Never promise or guarantee returns.
Build your brand on honesty, area knowledge and genuine referrals.

cards.prompt: Write the three sentences you want past clients to say about you in five years. Then write one habit for each that you will start this month to earn it.

quiz.question: Which is a warning sign of a property scam?
options: A written agreement with clear dates
A lawyer reviewing documents
Receipts for every payment
Guaranteed profit with pressure to pay today
quiz.explanation: Guaranteed returns and pressure to pay quickly are classic scam signs. Normal deals allow time for checks.

quiz.question: Where should you check a project's approval status?
options: Only in the project's brochure, since developers must print their approvals there
Directly with the relevant development authority
From the developer's social media page
From a dealer who is selling files
quiz.explanation: Brochures and ads may not be reliable. Confirm approval status directly with the relevant authority.

quiz.question: What is the best reply when a client asks about the exact fees for a transfer?
options: Check the current rules with the authority or a qualified lawyer
Quote the fee you heard last year, because fees rarely change much
Say there are no fees at all
Tell them to ignore fees for now
quiz.explanation: Fees and procedures change and vary by case, so direct the client to the right source.

quiz.question: Why should the seller's identity match the ownership record?
options: To decide the asking price, since the owner's name affects the market value
To choose the listing photos
To confirm the seller really owns the property
To calculate the agent's fee
quiz.explanation: Someone who is not the owner, or lacks proper authority, cannot sell safely. Matching identity is a basic check.

quiz.question: Which ad is honest?
options: 'Guaranteed double profit in a year!'
'Recent photos; please verify approvals yourself'
'Fully approved' with no way to check
'Bait price for a house that is sold'
quiz.explanation: Honest ads describe the real property and invite proper checks. Misleading ads promise what cannot be proven.

quiz.question: A plot file is priced far below similar properties and payment is asked to a personal account. What should you advise?
options: Pay a small amount to hold it
Buy quickly before the price rises
Ask a friend to pay on your behalf
Stop and verify everything before paying
quiz.explanation: These are strong red flags. Stop, verify with the relevant authority and get legal advice before any payment.

quiz.question: What is the base of a strong personal brand?
options: Expensive advertising
Many followers
A fancy logo
Honesty
quiz.explanation: Honesty supports everything else. Without it, content and presence do not build lasting trust.

quiz.question: Which personal brand habit is acceptable?
options: Writing fake reviews from friends
Asking happy clients for genuine feedback
Promising guaranteed returns in posts
Using another agent's listings as yours
quiz.explanation: Genuine feedback is honest and valuable. Fake reviews and false claims damage trust and may break rules.

quiz.question: You represent both the buyer and the seller in one deal. What should you do?
options: Tell both sides clearly and get their agreement
Keep it secret so nobody worries, as long as you treat both sides fairly
Charge only the side that pays more
Tell only the seller
quiz.explanation: Being open about dual representation lets both sides decide whether they are comfortable and avoids hidden conflicts.

quiz.question: Why should agents avoid promising property returns?
options: Returns are always guaranteed anyway
Buyers never care about returns
Property values can go down as well as up
Promises are only allowed for flats
quiz.explanation: No one can guarantee future property values. Promising returns misleads clients and can cause real losses.

bank.question: A new agent tells every caller 'yes, we have exactly what you want' without asking questions. What is the main long-term risk?
options: Too many qualified buyers to handle properly in the same week
Broken promises that destroy trust and referrals
Lower portal advertising costs
Faster deals with fewer viewings
